title: Is the smith machine completely useless？
summary: He argues the Smith machine is a poor and even dangerous teaching tool for beginners. Its fixed vertical path stops the body from adjusting the bar path or saving bad form, it is easier than free weights so beginners overload it, and it doesn't train stabilizers. It is useful for advanced lifters who want to target muscles heavy without balancing (front squats, rows, sissy squats), and its square top frame makes his favorite chin-up bar.

claims.claim: A Smith machine is a rack with a barbell fixed to it that only moves straight up and down.
Beginners are often told to learn bench or squat on the Smith machine first; he thinks it should be reserved for advanced lifters and beginners shouldn't touch it.
The Smith machine doesn't teach compound movements, doesn't build the musculature needed for them, and is more dangerous than a free barbell.
With free weights the body moves around the bar to keep the bar path vertical, so form can be corrected.

A good bar path is as vertical as possible, but the body doesn't move in a straight line: you press back toward the rack on bench, and the hips shift on squats and deadlifts. A Smith machine imposes its own path.

In a Smith machine you can't adjust out of a bad position: if your upper back rounds in a squat you can't recover it as with a barbell, and you end up doing a loaded good morning that is terrible for the back.
The Smith machine is much easier than free weights because the fixed straight path lets you apply all your strength and the bar is stabilized on both sides.
Because the Smith is easier, beginners stack weight, then carry inflated loads and poor form to free weights and get injured.
Smith machine strength doesn't transfer well to free weights: prime movers may get stronger, but the core and stabilizers aren't taxed, raising acute and chronic injury risk on compound lifts.
He only partly agrees that gyms should replace Smith machines with racks, because the Smith has uses.
The Smith machine's real use: advanced lifters targeting specific muscles with heavy weight without worrying about stabilization.
Smith machine front squats work well: you can use the bodybuilder crossed-arm rack without fear of dropping the bar, keep a very vertical torso and focus on the quads, replacing a hack squat machine.
Smith machine rows standing on a box turn the row into a pure isolation movement with no leg or lower back help, stricter than cable rows where people swing.
Sissy squats on the Smith machine are fine, but these lifts aren't for beginners anyway.
His favorite Smith use: supinated, medium-grip chin-ups on the thick square top frame with a false or wrapped grip; easy on the grip, taxing on forearms, the best lat movement he has ever found.
Pronated pull-ups on the Smith frame feel terrible on his biceps and forearms; only supinated chin-ups feel great there.

Verdict: the Smith machine is useless for beginners and most people, who should focus on free weights; advanced lifters who know what they're doing can use it, but someone who has never free-benched has no business doing 225 on the Smith.
